Name: lexical_scaffolding
Title: Does Naming Help Thinking? Testing Whether Giving LLMs a Word for a Concept Bootstraps Non-Linguistic Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Introducing a concise linguistic label (a coined word plus definition) for a latent, initially-unnamed regularity causally improves an LLM's ability to reason about that regularity on non-linguistic/structural tasks, more than an information-matched but unlabeled exposure. This tests a Whorfian 'language-as-cognitive-tool' hypothesis in LLMs: the act of lexicalizing/naming a concept, beyond conveying the same information, provides a reusable compression handle that scaffolds reasoning—revealing that part of LLM 'intelligence' is unlocked by having words for things.
Related Work: Xu et al. (2024, reverse-dictionary probe) show conceptual inference predicts general reasoning and that description->word prompting can facilitate commonsense reasoning, but they do not causally isolate the naming/lexicalization act from the underlying information, nor test transfer to non-linguistic structural tasks. Concept-Aware Fine-Tuning (Chen et al. 2025) modifies training to treat multi-token phrases as units but studies architecture/training efficiency, not causal cognitive scaffolding from labels. In-context learning and analogy work show examples help, but none isolate whether *coining a name* for an abstraction (vs. providing the same abstraction unnamed) yields extra reasoning benefit. Cognitive-science 'label-as-invitation-to-form-categories' (Waxman/Lupyan) motivates the hypothesis; we are the first to operationalize and causally test it in LLMs with matched-information controls.
Abstract: Human cognition is shaped by having words for concepts: a single label can compress a complex regularity into a reusable cognitive handle. Do large language models benefit similarly? We ask whether the act of *naming* a concept—beyond merely conveying its defining information—causally improves an LLM's reasoning about that concept on non-linguistic, structural tasks. We construct families of novel latent regularities (e.g., a specific graph motif, a numeric predicate like 'divisible-by-7-and-prime-adjacent', a spatial configuration, a rule over synthetic sequences) that are unlikely to have pre-existing lexicalization. For each, we compare three information-matched interventions delivered in-context (and via LoRA finetuning): (1) NAMED—a coined word plus one-line definition ('a splorb is X'); (2) DESCRIBED—the same definition without a reusable label, phrased so the concept must be re-derived each use; (3) EXEMPLIFIED-ONLY—matched positive/negative examples with no explicit rule. We then measure downstream reasoning: classification of new instances, multi-step composition ('is this both a splorb and a blicket?'), counterfactual manipulation, and transfer to a re-skinned domain. We hypothesize a NAMED > DESCRIBED > EXEMPLIFIED ordering that grows with concept compositional depth, and that the benefit correlates with how compressible the label makes intermediate reasoning traces (measured by trace length and repeated-label reuse). Mechanistic probes test whether the coined token acquires a stable, reusable internal representation. Results would show that lexicalization is not neutral packaging but a causal cognitive scaffold in LLMs, informing prompt design, curriculum construction, and theories of language-thought coupling in AI.
Experiments: 1) CONCEPT CONSTRUCTION: Build ~40 novel latent concepts across 4 domains (graph/relational motifs, numeric predicates, spatial configurations, synthetic-sequence rules), each with a generator producing positive/negative instances and compositional queries. Verify concepts are 'unnamed' (no common English word) and not solvable by memorized shortcuts via a no-instruction baseline. 2) INTERVENTION CONDITIONS (information-matched): NAMED (coined nonce word + one-line definition), DESCRIBED (identical definitional content but rephrased each usage without a reusable single label, and queries must restate the rule), EXEMPLIFIED-ONLY (k matched labeled examples, no rule). Control k/tokens so total input information is matched; validate matching with human/automated info-content checks. 3) EVALUATION TASKS per concept: (a) new-instance classification accuracy; (b) COMPOSITION—conjunctions/negations/nesting of 2-3 coined concepts; (c) COUNTERFACTUAL—'modify this instance minimally so it becomes a splorb'; (d) TRANSFER—apply concept in a re-skinned surface domain. 4) MODELS: Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2 at 2 sizes each; both pure prompting and light LoRA finetuning (few hundred examples per concept) to test whether naming benefit persists under gradient learning. 5) SCALING WITH DEPTH: measure how the NAMED advantage grows with compositional depth (single vs 2-vs 3-concept queries)—predict widening gap for NAMED due to reusable compression. 6) TRACE ANALYSIS: with CoT enabled, measure reasoning-trace length and count of coined-label reuses; test whether NAMED yields shorter traces via label reuse and whether trace compression mediates accuracy (mediation analysis). 7) MECHANISTIC PROBE: train linear probes / measure representation stability of the coined nonce token's hidden state across contexts; test whether NAMED induces a more consistent, decodable concept representation than DESCRIBED. METRICS: accuracy per task/condition, NAMED-DESCRIBED and NAMED-EXEMPLIFIED effect sizes with mixed-effects models (random effects for concept and model), compositional-depth interaction coefficient, trace length, mediation effect, probe decodability/consistency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Perfect information matching between NAMED and DESCRIBED is hard; the label itself adds a tiny bit of information—we mitigate by using content-identical definitions and validating info content, and by including the EXEMPLIFIED control. 2) Benefits may reflect mere token-level anchoring/attention convenience rather than deep 'cognitive scaffolding'; the compositional-depth and mechanistic-probe analyses help distinguish these but interpretation remains partly caveated. 3) Coined nonce words may tokenize inconsistently, adding noise—we select tokenizer-friendly labels and report tokenization as a covariate. 4) Effects could be small or model/size-dependent; multiple models/sizes and effect-size reporting address this. 5) Synthetic concepts may not generalize to naturalistic knowledge; we include diverse domains and a transfer task but acknowledge limited ecological validity. 6) Finetuning may wash out prompting differences; we treat the prompting-vs-finetuning contrast itself as an informative result about where naming matters.
